Prediction Error & Q‑Distance in the Fixed 3‑Arm Pilot

How each participant's belief state drifted from indifference over the course of the task, and how that drift relates to win‑stay/lose–shift behavior.

01The question

The request: for every participant in the fixed pilot — the task variant where all three slot machines are offered on every trial, i.e. a genuine free‑choice 3‑arm bandit — plot the trial‑by‑trial prediction error from a reinforcement‑learning model of their choices, one panel per subject. Alongside it, on the same axes, plot a second quantity: the summed squared distance of all three of the model's Q‑values from 0.5, per trial — a running measure of how far the model's beliefs about the machines have moved away from the naive 50/50 prior. The lab's existing 3‑arm model was to be used, matched to the 3‑arm structure of this dataset.

02Locating the model and the data

Before writing anything, the fixed‑pilot CSVs were checked directly: the unavailable_keys field is empty on every trial for every subject, confirming this is the true always‑3‑arm variant. The key→location→color mapping (arrowup/top‑center/blue, arrowleft/bottom‑left/green, arrowright/bottom‑right/red) turned out to be fixed across the whole session and across every subject, so a choice key can serve directly as an arm identity.

The lab's abkd_3arm.stan model (nicknamed M1) matched the task exactly: Q‑values initialized at 0.5 per arm, updated by classic Rescorla‑Wagner on the chosen arm only, persisting across blocks (never reset mid‑session), plus a decaying perseveration term that doesn't affect the Q‑trajectory itself. Fitted subject‑level learning rates (α) from this model already existed in analysis/param_estimation, fit on the 18‑subject snapshot of the fixed pilot that existed at the time.

03Replaying each subject's choices

For every subject, their real trial sequence (task = gambling_choice, training block excluded, invalid trials dropped) was replayed through Rescorla‑Wagner using that subject's own fitted α, tracking two quantities at each trial, before that trial's update:

  • Prediction error — reward − Q(chosen arm)
  • Q‑distance — Σ (Qa − 0.5)² summed over all three arms

This produced the first figure: one facet per subject, prediction error and Q‑distance overlaid on the same trial axis in the lab's Okabe‑Ito palette — blue for prediction error, orange for Q‑distance.

04Connecting drift to behavior

The next ask was to relate that Q‑distance to win‑stay/lose–shift (WSLS) behavior. Rather than invent a new definition, the lab's existing method was reused: analysis/wm_wsls/wm_wsls.R already computes a per‑subject WSLS effect size as the slope of a lag‑1 logistic regression, stay ~ previous_reward, deliberately keeping trial pairs that cross block boundaries (the lab's stated convention). Each subject's mean Q‑distance across all their trials was plotted against that WSLS slope.

Mid‑session complication

When asked to re‑display the figures later, they no longer existed: the working container had been reset, and the feature branch had been rebuilt from a much newer main. In the interim, the lab's own work had moved on substantially — the fixed pilot had grown from 18 to 35 participants, and abkd_3arm/M1 had been retired in favor of a new family of models, with no saved posterior draws for any of them on this dataset yet. Rather than silently show a stale result, this was surfaced directly and confirmed before rebuilding.

05Rebuilding on the current model

Of the new model family, classic_qval_and_unchosen_eval_zero is the direct successor to M1: the same classic Rescorla‑Wagner Q‑learning core, with a streak‑based perseveration trace in place of the old decay term — mechanically identical where it matters for this analysis. Since no Bayesian fit existed yet for this model on the 35‑subject dataset, and running a full hierarchical Stan fit was impractical mid‑session, per‑subject learning rates were instead estimated by direct maximum‑likelihood optimization of the same choice model (fit_alpha_mle.R) — a point estimate rather than a posterior median, but driving exactly the same Q‑trajectory the task calls for. Both figures were then regenerated across all 35 subjects.

A second, unrelated surprise turned up while pushing this work: the remote branch had itself been force‑reset, restoring the two original 18‑subject commits on top of the old codebase. The histories were merged — keeping the rebuilt 35‑subject content as the result, while leaving the earlier commits reachable rather than discarding them.

06Cleaning the WSLS scatter

Two subjects sat far outside the rest of the scatter. Both turned out to be the same statistical artifact from opposite directions: each showed near‑total consistency in staying or switching after a given outcome (one stayed after every single loss), which drives a per‑subject logistic regression toward quasi‑complete separation — a coefficient that diverges toward ±∞ and carries no real information about effect size, rather than a genuine extreme WSLS tendency. Both were removed on request.
